sm: Ben Shapiro opens by describing an exchange between Kevin O'Leary, the Shark Tank investor, and a group of Gen Z workers on the Jubilee show Surrounded. A young participant accused O'Leary of bullying kids to work harder instead of challenging industry. Shapiro says this reflects a common view among young people that hard work cannot get them ahead and that the system must be torn down. He notes that online comments sided with the young people, calling O'Leary out of touch and saying America is not a meritocracy. O'Leary had suggested that mistreated workers should quit and go elsewhere.

Shapiro tells his own story. He grew up in a small Burbank house with his parents and three sisters, went to UCLA, paid his own way through Harvard Law, and left a law firm after ten months for a job at one-third of the pay at Talk Radio Network. There he got up at 4:30 every morning to cut audio, did legal work, and later ghostwrote, sometimes holding four or five jobs at once. He calls that slow rise in wealth a normal American trajectory that is open to young people. He argues the despair comes largely from highly educated, downwardly mobile people who expected a degree to guarantee wealth, and from a false history in which grandparents and boomers had it easy.

Shapiro plays a Gen Z participant who says the American dream was stolen. She cites about forty thousand dollars of student debt, unaffordable homes and vacations, productivity up ninety percent since 1979 against wages up thirty percent, and falling unionization. Shapiro responds that young people are not economically worse off than their parents, since today's houses are larger and interest rates lower than in 1982. He says productivity gains come mostly from technology, and that college costs rose because government subsidized demand. A second participant demands evidence that America is the best economy. Shapiro cites a Cato study that found ninety-three percent of children from the bottom quintile ended up better off than their parents. He also says the upper middle class tripled from ten to thirty-one percent of families between 1979 and 2024, that mobility is lowest in countries like Peru, South Africa, China and Brazil, and that Denmark's mobility depends on taxes Americans would not accept.

Shapiro criticizes Gen Z for condemning the wealthy rather than asking how to become wealthy. A participant says the top one percent hold a large share of national wealth and that people starve in America. Shapiro says the malnutrition deaths are mostly among elderly people in nursing homes and reflect a care problem, not an income problem. He explains that the wealth gap between older and younger people simply reflects time spent accumulating, using his parents and his younger sister as examples. He plays O'Leary saying that no one becomes rich overnight and that success takes a decade of sacrifice. Shapiro adds that wealth comes from risk, outsized ideas, or very long hard work.

Shapiro then discusses a viral clip of an unarmed security guard who works eighty hours a week and pays fifty-five percent of his income in rent. The guard says there is no room for advancement, and O'Leary presses him on lateral moves and side work. Shapiro says the options are thrift, a lateral career move, or a side business, and that there is no system in which people stop worrying. He calls the Gen Z attitude nihilism and says the idea that most decisions are out of your hands feeds a volatile politics. Finally he turns to a participant who warns that AI will eliminate up to half of jobs, citing Dario Amodei and Sam Altman. Shapiro says people cannot complain both that everything is unaffordable and that a machine making goods cheaply will take their jobs.

Shapiro cites a New York Times piece on student protests and riots in France and India over a broken meritocratic bargain. He says the bargain never promised riches for a liberal arts degree, since meritocracy requires productive skills. He argues the country is producing an overeducated, downwardly mobile class that becomes revolutionary, quoting Thomas Sowell on degrees without economically valuable skills. He points to Mike Rowe's campaign to boost the trades and defense industry jobs. Shapiro notes that Gen Z is the most educated generation ever, with about half finishing college, and says the fix is free markets and honest advice such as moving to a state with more jobs, as he moved for his wife's medical school. He asks whether people would rather be happy and right or unhappy and revolutionary.

Shapiro says Democratic-run cities show the cost of over-promising. Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson lost his third chief financial officer in months, who said she could not vouch for accurate city finances, and Johnson said he put migrant funding into black-owned businesses. Shapiro cites ProPublica that Chicago owes about fifty-five billion dollars and will spend 3.9 billion on debt service. He mentions Ro Khanna's proposed seventeen-hundred-dollar check over the Iran war, which Shapiro prices at about 581 billion dollars, and a New York Times finding that progressive candidates underperformed moderates. He also touches on rainbow sidewalks in Texas and a Florida town canceling St. Patrick's Day.

Shapiro covers the Nvidia chip controversy. The Commerce Department will now require licenses for advanced chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, after Treasury and State pushed the rule over Howard Lutnick. Trump defended his officials, and J.D. Vance told Laura Ingraham he does not know whether Alice Huang was a spy. Shapiro notes Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares more than a hundred times. He then covers Microsoft and bank outages and the unfixed FAA system, where Vance said Congress must provide funds, and Sean Duffy said more money is needed, with fifty billion dollars now requested.

Last, Shapiro reports CNN's account that Iran is developing options for a dirty bomb or chemical attack in Washington aimed at senior officials, though not as an imminent plot. Scott Bessent is reportedly living on a military base because of threats. Shapiro cites Senator Tim Sheehy's Wall Street Journal piece arguing that the Iran war is unpopular but defeat would be worse. Shapiro worries Trump is trying to appease China and Russia ahead of a meeting with the Chinese later this week.
